data.title: The COLA wars are coming for Social Security
data.description:
By Brett Arends

As the entire program nears financial insolvency, the annual cost-of-living adjustment comes under scrutiny

If they change your COLA, will you be ready?

The annual cost-of-living adjustment, known as COLA, may soon be capped, curtailed, means-tested or scrapped altogether under various proposals being actively considered in Washington, D.C.

That's because policymakers are facing the program's looming financial insolvency, which under current forecasts is expected to hit within several years.

One proposal under review would scrap annual cost-of-living adjustments altogether for beneficiaries with higher incomes. The Social Security Administration reckons the government could fill about a third of the program's long-term financial shortfall by ending COLAs for those making more than about $117,300 a year (for single tax-filers) or $234,600 (for joint filers), along with reducing the annual COLA for everyone else.

The Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget, an independent think tank, offers a more modest idea: Simply limit the dollar value of COLAs for higher earners to the amount received by median beneficiaries. That would work at around $75 a month for next year's COLA. (The median and the average are very similar in this case.)

So a couple with a $3,300 monthly Social Security benefit, which places them on the cusp of the top 10%, would get a 2027 benefit increase of $75 instead of the $122 they currently expect.

Another idea would be still more progressive: Give everyone the dollar amount received by some lower earners. This was first proposed by former Rep. Tim Penny, now co-chair of the CRFB, back in the 1980s.

For example, using calculations from the Urban Institute's Karen Smith, the CRFB estimates that Social Security could cut its long-term shortfall by about half by limiting everyone to the dollar increase received by those at the 20th percentile. (The way to conceptualize the 20th percentile is to imagine lining all Social Security beneficiaries up in a really, really, really long line, from those getting the least at one end to those getting the most at the other, and then finding the person who is 20% of the way along from the lowest earner.)

And they reckon the program could cut its shortfall by 40% by limiting COLAs to the dollar amount received by those at the 30th percentile.

That would mean everyone would get a 2027 COLA of just $50 per month, regardless of their current benefit levels.

Other proposals making the rounds may be politically easier, but they are more egregious as well. One involves cutting Social Security's COLA for everyone. The Social Security Administration has run the numbers on cutting the annual COLA across the board by one full percentage point a year, or by half a point, or by changing how it's calculated, replacing the current CPI inflation calculation with a less generous rate known as the "chained" CPI. The Social Security Administration estimates this would cut the COLA by a third of a percentage point a year.

The problem with these ideas is that they would effectively fall hardest on those who get the least, and who are most dependent on Social Security.

Howard Lutnick, the billionaire commerce secretary, bragged last year that if the Social Security Administration stopped sending checks to his mother-in-law she wouldn't complain. But that's not true for 90% of beneficiaries. Many depend on Social Security to live. Cutting their annual COLA by the same percentage as the annual COLA for Lutnick's mother-in-law probably appeals to a certain group of people, but they are a tiny minority.

If you object to any changes to the COLA calculations, then how will you fix Social Security's finances?

Eliminating the taxable-income ceiling for Social Security taxes, set to rise to $192,300 next year, would cause a huge effective jump of 12.4 percentage points in the marginal federal tax rate among higher earners.

Raising the retirement age would be a benefit cut across the board, and would most hurt those who do more physically demanding jobs, many of which are lower paid.

Some people suggest that we could help address the problem by actually levying some taxes - any taxes at all - on people as rich as Jeff Bezos and Elon Musk, whose personal wealth recently hit $1 trillion. And by making private-equity managers, hedge-fund managers, venture capitalists and other Wall Street types just pay income taxes like the rest of us.

But people making those suggestions are probably all communists and can be ignored.

Other options include getting in a time machine, going back 30 years, and voting against the 2001, 2017 and 2025 tax cuts, as well as the massive federal deficits of the global financial crisis and the COVID crisis. Without all that, if we had kept the income taxes we had when President Bill Clinton left office in 2001, there would be no federal budget crisis and Social Security could just be shored up from general funds.

If you don't have a time machine, there's one other option: waiting for the magical "waste, fraud and abuse" fairy to turn up and shower us all with trillions in free money. We've been waiting since Ronald Reagan announced her imminent arrival way back in 1980, and we haven't seen her yet. But here's hoping!

-Brett Arends

data.title: Are we spending our retirement money in the right order? Our plan is: Social Security, annuities, cash - then IRA.
data.description:
By Beth Pinsker

Spending all your cash first can make your income surge in later years

You have too many decisions to make in retirement to get every one of them exactly right.

Got a question about retirement? Fill out our questionnaire or write to me directly at beth.pinsker@marketwatch.com (please put "Fix My Portfolio" in the subject line).

Dear Fix My Portfolio,

I think I'm doing it right but I have a question: How do we avoid the late-life high tax and Medicare penalties (IRMAA) that you have talked about?

We are 72 and lucky to be comfortable with no debt. My wife waited to take Social Security at 66 and I waited until 70. That brings us about $90,000 a year. We have fixed annuities that bring in $22,000 a year.

We have $500,000 in cash from downsizing, and $800,000 in home equity in our paid-off house. I haven't yet touched my rollover IRA that has $900,000, invested in a mix of funds and bonds, or a Roth IRA at $180,000 (this is where I'm aggressive in stocks). l also have life insurance with a surrender value of $750,000.

I have been assuming that my spend-down sequence is what we've been doing: Social Security, annuities and cash first, then move to spending down the IRA when I have to start withdrawals at 73, then Roth last, leaving the insurance as our self-funded long-term-care policy. I figure we have a few big travels left in us before large expenditures stop.

I understand the logic of spending pretax IRA money first and converting money to Roth, but I'm not sure where that fits in for us. If we don't make those moves, are we, in fact, doing it right?

Double Checker

Dear Double Checker,

Yes, congratulations, you have done retirement right! That is not to say that you've done it perfectly, because there are thousands of decisions to make along the way and not all of them can be absolutely optimal. What overrides everything is that you have enough for a comfortable life today and that you can withstand emergencies down the road, and you look in pretty good shape for that.

Now, on to the task of optimizing as much as you can.

Running the numbers

Thank you for providing enough details to flesh out some real sense of your options. You can't really get into the nitty-gritty unless you are looking at real numbers. And you can't really do this with back-of-the-envelope math. That's not to say that you need to pay an adviser either for a plan or for ongoing management, but you do need access to some advanced financial calculators.

I was able to take your details and run them through the free version of the software on the Boldin platform, and that made the picture a little clearer.

The first thing I looked at was whether your spending plan offered you enough cash on hand for your current living expenses, and what would happen if you increased that. I allowed for $10,000 a year for special spending on top of your monthly budget for travel for 10 years, so you would build in a little fun.

With a regular budget of $10,000 a month for your everyday needs, your chance of success - meaning, your money outlives you - was 99%, according to the sketch of your situation in Boldin. That might seem great to you, but it might actually be too much winning. In financial-planning software math, a 99% chance of success means that you're likely to have more money left after you die than you have now. You didn't mention a legacy plan, but unless you have a purpose for that much money, you can spend a little more and still be considered cautious.

If you up your budget to $12,000 a month, for instance, Boldin still gives you a 77% chance of success, and you'd still be projected to have several million dollars at age 97. But go to $15,000 a month, and your chances of success dip below 50%. So those are the guardrails to consider - spend between $10,000 and $15,000 a month. Then watch and adjust as you go along.

Spend-down order

Between Social Security and your annuity, you have at least $9,000 a month covered for now. It may be less as you go along if, sadly, one spouse predeceases the other. It's not a comfortable thing to talk about, but when you look at retirement numbers, you have to realistically consider the possibility.

When your RMDs start next year, you're going to have to take out roughly $34,000 as a required minimum distribution. This is why many advisers actually caution against the kind of strategy you're using, where you don't touch that IRA money until RMD age and you spend your other money first.

If you are in a low tax bracket after retirement and you are already 591/2, it can help smooth your taxes if you start with those pretax funds first. The reason for this is that if you wait and then only take RMDs, your withdrawals are likely to be below the rate of growth in the account, and so your balance will likely continue to grow. The RMD percentage also grows as you age, so the amount you are forced to take out will go up over time, and it may become a tax thorn in your side.

So much taxable money taken out could eventually push you over the income limit for the Medicare surcharges known as IRMAA, which start at $222,000 for a married couple. It could also increase the percentage of your Social Security that is taxed. Again, sorry to bring this up, but if there's one spouse and the same amount of money, the IRMAA threshold is currently $111,000 for an individual.

Boldin's "Wellness Scorecard" gives you mostly high marks overall, but the one place it marks you as vulnerable is in the category of Roth conversions. One way to solve the RMD tax problem is to use some of the $500,000 cash you have to pay the tax bill that you would incur if you were to convert some of your IRA to Roth. In that way, you would have a lower balance in your tax-deferred account, and you'd have more flexibility in later years to use that money tax-free.

But it's not a clear path. Roth conversions are all about paying the tax when your rate is lowest. The free portion of Boldin does not simulate Roth conversion activity - you have to pay for that level of analysis. I was able to ask Nancy Gates, Boldin's financial experience principal and education manager, how you could approach this decision. Her main advice was to proceed cautiously and work out a multiyear solution where you might convert small amounts, like $40,000 a year for four years.

There is a risk in overconverting. If you deplete your IRA down to nothing and have a long-term-care event in your 90s, then you might miss your best tax opportunity, which is to pay for that out of your tax-deferred account and offset it with a huge deduction for medical expenses.

"You don't want to tilt the seesaw too far," Gates said.

So before you proceed with your plan, try to work your numbers through various calculators and see what works best for you. Your best path may be a combination of spending - taking a third of your excess budget needs from your IRA, a third from the cash and a third from the Roth, rather than plowing through them sequentially.

You can also join the Retirement conversation in our Facebook community: Retire Better with MarketWatch.

data.title: Nephron Pharmaceuticals Announces Leadership Transition
data.description:
Nephron Pharmaceuticals Announces Leadership Transition

Lou Kennedy departs from CEO role; Haywood Miller appointed Interim CEO

Company remains focused on executing its transformation strategy and growth priorities while continuing to deliver safe, effective medications to customers and the patients they serve

Nephron LLC and its subsidiaries (“Nephron” or the “Company”) today announced the departure of Lou Kennedy from her role as Chief Executive Officer. Haywood Miller has been appointed Interim Chief Executive Officer, effective immediately.

Nephron enters this next chapter with the strong support of its secured lenders, who share confidence in the Company’s transformation strategy, growth priorities, long-standing customer relationships, and resilient manufacturing footprint. The Company remains focused on executing its transformation strategy and growth priorities, while continuing to deliver safe, effective medications to customers and their patients.

“I want to thank Lou for her leadership and her many years of service to Nephron,” said Richard Shinder, Nephron’s independent manager. “We are pleased to welcome Haywood Miller, whose operational expertise and deep familiarity of Nephron’s business makes him the right leader to advance the Company’s transformation, and execute on its growth initiatives.”

Mr. Miller, who brings more than 30 years of leadership experience in both the pharmaceutical manufacturing and healthcare industries, has a strong understanding of Nephron and its business, having served in an advisory capacity to the Company over the past several months as a Managing Director at Berkeley Research Group. As he assumes his new role, he will continue to work closely with Nephron’s leadership team to further strengthen operations, invest in the business and its people, while upholding the high standards of quality and reliability customers expect.

“Nephron has a strong foundation built on an exceptional team, trusted customer relationships, and world-class manufacturing capabilities, and the opportunity ahead is significant,” said Haywood Miller, Interim CEO of Nephron. “I look forward to working alongside our team to build on that foundation, execute on our growth and transformation strategy, and continue serving as a dependable source of high-quality medicines for providers nationwide.” The Company has taken deliberate steps to ensure an orderly transition, with clear continuity across manufacturing, compliance, quality, supply, and customer relationships. The Company’s operations continue as usual.

About Nephron Pharmaceuticals

A West Columbia, S.C.-based company, Nephron develops and produces safe, affordable sterile pharmaceutical products in a state of the art GMP-compliant manufacturing facility. The company also operates an industry-leading 503B Outsourcing Facility division which produces pre-filled sterile syringes, luer-lock vials, IV bottles and IV bags for hospitals across America, in an effort to alleviate drug shortage needs. For more information, please visit www.nephronpharm.com.

C Street Advisory Group
nephron@thecstreet.com

data.title: Microsoft wants to make AI cheaper. Will investors actually see the savings?
data.description:
By Jurica Dujmovic

Microsoft is betting that its custom chips can lower costs, but the AI equation is more complicated than that

Microsoft is expanding efforts with its Maia chip business.

Microsoft wants to make artificial intelligence cheaper to run. For investors trying to judge the return on its enormous infrastructure spending, that sounds encouraging.

But a lower computing bill for each task leaves an important question unanswered: How much of the savings will Microsoft (MSFT) actually keep?

Some of the money saved could become pure profit. Some could reach customers through lower prices. Some could finance more ambitious AI services that consume the extra capacity. Microsoft's new chip puts all three possibilities in play.

Earlier this week, Microsoft announced plans to expand its Maia systems to multigigawatt deployments starting in 2027, making them its primary infrastructure for inference across its products and services. Inference is what happens when a trained AI model answers a question or works through a task.

Diversifying beyond expensive chips made by Nvidia (NVDA) and doing more with its own custom chips could be a real opportunity for Microsoft to improve its AI economics. The investment case depends on turning that engineering progress into profitable customer demand while controlling the capital required to serve it.

Don't miss: Don't ditch tech stocks just yet. Make these moves to take advantage of the latest AI reset.

Maia 300, scheduled to begin production deployments in 2027, is central to that effort. Microsoft expects it to deliver 40% more tokens - pieces of information that AI models process and generate - per megawatt than leading systems based on graphics processing units.

That is a company projection, and the announcement does not identify the competing systems behind the comparison. Investors should also resist reading it as a promise of 40% lower costs. Power-efficiency measures only part of the expense of delivering AI. Chips, memory, networking, buildings, software and maintenance all have to be paid for.

Even the power arithmetic needs care. Producing 40% more output with the same power would imply roughly 29% less energy per token under comparable operating conditions. Neither figure establishes the savings on Microsoft's total bill.

Nevertheless, the business logic is compelling. Microsoft sells applications and cloud services, giving it opportunities to design infrastructure around work its customers already perform. It says Maia 200 is already serving production workloads, including Microsoft Copilot, the company's AI assistant. The successor therefore builds on an operating program, although its promised performance remains ahead.

The financial stakes are substantial. In the June quarter, Microsoft Cloud revenue reached $59.3 billion, up 27% from a year earlier. Across the company, cash additions to property and equipment totaled $35.8 billion, compared with $17.1 billion a year earlier. Those figures cover more than AI, but they show the scale of the business and investment that efficiency improvements must support.

The clearest route to shareholder gains would be lower costs for serving existing customers. If Microsoft can deliver the same useful service for less while maintaining prices, it retains more revenue after delivery expenses. Repeated across millions of interactions, modest savings could become meaningful.

Consider this example: A service brings in $100 and costs $60 to deliver, leaving $40 before other expenses. Reduce delivery costs to $50, and that margin rises to $50. But if competitive pressure also reduces revenue to $90, the margin stays at $40. Technical progress has benefited the customer without increasing the provider's profit dollars on that sale.

That second outcome can still be attractive. Lower prices could bring in customers who previously found the service too expensive. Higher volume could then generate more total profit. The question is whether the additional business compensates for the lower price and any extra infrastructure required.

A third possibility is that Microsoft keeps prices steady while giving customers more AI work for their money. An assistant might examine more documents, check its answers more thoroughly or complete longer assignments. The customer receives a better product, but heavier usage can absorb the savings from cheaper computing.

That makes cost per useful completed task more revealing than cost per token alone. A system that produces inexpensive answers but requires repeated corrections can be costly to use. A more demanding system might be worth its higher computing bill if it reliably finishes work that customers value.

For Nvidia investors, Maia raises a broader question: How much pricing power can a supplier retain when its biggest customers develop credible alternatives? Microsoft does not need to replace every Nvidia chip to strengthen its negotiating position. It needs an alternative that performs enough of its work reliably and economically to make shifting orders a realistic option.

That could affect Nvidia well before any outright decline in sales. Microsoft could direct more of its next round of spending toward its own chips, or use that option to negotiate better terms on GPUs. Nvidia's revenue could still grow in an expanding market while it captures a smaller share of a customer's budget or accepts lower margins to secure business. Investors should distinguish those outcomes: Continued sales growth would not, by itself, settle the question of bargaining power.

The shift is not automatic. Microsoft must demonstrate that Maia's savings survive the costs of development, deployment and adapting software to run on it. A chip that performs well on selected tasks is useful, but its negotiating value depends on how much spending Microsoft can realistically redirect. Nvidia can defend its position by making its systems more valuable overall, including through performance, software support and reliability.

The question, then, is how much of AI's future growth Nvidia can capture, and on what terms. Successful custom chips could let Microsoft retain more of the money it earns from AI, while putting pressure on the prices Nvidia can charge. Both companies could benefit from rising demand, but shareholders should watch how the profits are divided.

See also: Microsoft hits a big milestone that solidifies its revival

For Microsoft shareholders, three measures will help show whether those potential savings are becoming financial gains.

First, cloud margins alongside growth as deployment progresses. Improving margins with sustained demand would support the case that Microsoft is retaining some efficiency gains. Aggregate figures cannot isolate Maia's contribution, so management's explanation of infrastructure costs and product mix will matter.

Second, customer spending and retention. Lower prices or more generous usage allowances need to translate into durable business. Investors should look for customers who continue paying and renew their contracts after the initial enthusiasm fades.

Third, cash generation relative to investment. A more efficient chip can improve operating economics while a larger deployment consumes additional cash. Investors should compare operating cash flow, capital spending and financing commitments over several quarters, allowing for the timing of construction and equipment purchases.

Microsoft's announcement strengthens its case for controlling the cost of AI. It leaves open how the resulting benefits will be shared among customers, suppliers and shareholders. The strongest evidence will come when more useful AI services produce durable revenue and cash returns that justify the infrastructure behind them. That is the standard by which investors should judge Maia.

-Jurica Dujmovic

data.title: Property Management Expert Amy Reynolds Explains Rental Income Strategies in HelloNation
data.description:
Property Management Expert Amy Reynolds Explains Rental Income Strategies in HelloNation

Property Management Expert Amy Reynolds Explains Rental Income Strategies in HelloNation

PR Newswire

FAYETTEVILLE, N.C., Oct. 16, 2026

The Article Explains How Investors Can Evaluate Rental Income, Property Expenses, and Potential Profits Before Purchasing an Investment Property.

FAYETTEVILLE, N.C., Oct. 16, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- What should investors evaluate before purchasing an investment property? HelloNation has published an article that answers this question with insights from Amy Reynolds of ACE Real Estate & Property Management in Fayetteville, NC.

The article explains that estimating rental income accurately is one of the most important parts of evaluating an investment property. While a property may initially appear profitable, long-term rental profits often depend on local market conditions, vacancy trends, and total ownership costs. The article notes that careful financial planning can help investors avoid unrealistic expectations before deciding to buy.

According to the HelloNation article, one of the first steps in evaluating rental income is to compare similar rental homes in the same market. Investors are encouraged to review properties with similar layouts, square footage, condition, and neighborhood characteristics. Recently leased rental homes may offer a clearer picture of actual market demand than active listings alone. In Fayetteville, NC, rental prices may vary based on factors such as access to schools, local employers, and proximity to Fort Liberty.

The article also emphasizes the importance of studying vacancy trends before purchasing an investment property. Even homes with strong monthly rental income projections can become less profitable if vacancies occur frequently. Investors are encouraged to account for potential vacancy periods in their calculations rather than assuming continuous occupancy year-round. The article explains that conservative vacancy estimates often provide a more realistic view of annual cash flow.

Ownership expenses are another major focus. The HelloNation article explains that mortgage payments represent only part of the ongoing financial responsibilities associated with an investment property. Property taxes, insurance costs, maintenance, landscaping, repairs, and property management fees should all be included when calculating expected rental property profits. Older rental homes may require additional reserve funds due to aging systems or deferred maintenance.

The article also explains that newer investors commonly underestimate maintenance costs. Routine maintenance, appliance replacements, HVAC servicing, and tenant turnover expenses can gradually reduce rental income. Some property owners also maintain reserve funds for emergency repairs to reduce financial strain when unexpected issues arise. The article notes that accounting for these ownership expenses early may help investors better understand long-term profitability expectations.

Property management services are also discussed as part of a balanced investment strategy. The article explains that professional property management may include lease administration, tenant screening, maintenance coordination, rent collection, inspections, and communication support. Although these services reduce immediate monthly rental income, many investors view property management as valuable for supporting stable operations and reducing vacancy trends. The article notes that consistent oversight may also help preserve property condition and tenant retention.

For those evaluating opportunities in Fayetteville, NC, the article explains that rental income potential depends on several local market factors. Single-family rental homes near military housing demand may experience more stable interest rates, while other neighborhoods may show different pricing patterns. Property size, amenities, local supply levels, and condition all contribute to expected rental property profits.

The article also encourages investors to avoid relying solely on best-case projections. Inflated rental income estimates or underestimated ownership expenses can create financial challenges later. Instead, conservative financial analysis can help determine whether an investment property remains sustainable during slower market periods or when maintenance costs increase unexpectedly.

The article concludes that careful preparation before purchasing an investment property may help investors make more informed financial decisions. By reviewing comparable rental homes, studying vacancy trends, and fully accounting for ownership expenses, investors may better understand long-term rental property profits in Fayetteville, NC.

How to Estimate Rental Income Before Purchasing an Investment Property features insights from Amy Reynolds, a Property Management Expert in Fayetteville, North Carolina, on HelloNation.

data.title: HelloNation Examines Repair vs Replace HVAC Decisions With Insights From HVAC Expert Leslie Roe
data.description:
HelloNation Examines Repair vs Replace HVAC Decisions With Insights From HVAC Expert Leslie Roe

HelloNation Examines Repair vs Replace HVAC Decisions With Insights From HVAC Expert Leslie Roe

PR Newswire

TRAVERSE CITY, Mich., Nov. 20, 2026

The article outlines key factors that influence cost, efficiency, and long-term home comfort.

TRAVERSE CITY, Mich., Nov. 20, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- What should homeowners consider first when deciding between repair vs replace HVAC systems? The answer is explored in a HelloNation article that offers guidance and features insights from HVAC Expert Leslie Roe of Precision Plumbing and Heating Systems in Traverse City, Michigan.

The HelloNation article explains that HVAC system age is one of the most important factors in the repair-versus-replace decision. Systems typically last 10 to 15 years, and as HVAC systems age, the likelihood of costly breakdowns increases. The article notes that when a unit nears the end of its expected lifespan, replacement may offer more value than repeated furnace repair or temporary fixes.

Maintenance history also plays a central role in evaluating repair vs replace HVAC options. The article describes how a consistent maintenance history often leads to better performance and fewer disruptions. In contrast, poor maintenance history can lead to recurring HVAC issues that drive up repair costs over time. HVAC Expert Leslie Roe emphasizes in the article that recurring HVAC issues often signal that replacement should be considered more seriously.

The article also examines the type and severity of system problems. Minor issues, such as thermostat malfunctions or small leaks, may require only furnace repair or targeted service. However, multiple component failures and recurring HVAC issues often point to a system that can no longer operate efficiently. In these cases, the article explains that repair may provide only short-term relief, while AC replacement may offer a more stable long-term solution.

Energy use is another major factor discussed in the article. Older systems tend to lack modern heating and cooling efficiency, leading to higher monthly utility costs. The article highlights that upgrading to an AC replacement can significantly improve heating and cooling efficiency while reducing strain on the system. Improved heating and cooling efficiency not only lowers expenses but also enhances year-round home comfort.

Comfort and performance are closely tied to system condition. The article notes that uneven temperatures, weak airflow, and frequent cycling can reduce home comfort and signal deeper system problems. HVAC Expert Leslie Roe explains in the article that maintaining home comfort is often easier with newer systems designed for consistent performance. While furnace repair may temporarily restore function, long-term home comfort is often improved by replacement when systems are outdated.

Budget considerations are also addressed in the HelloNation article. Repair costs are usually lower at first, making furnace repair an appealing short-term option. However, the article explains that repeated repairs tied to recurring HVAC issues can quickly add up. AC replacement requires a higher upfront investment, but it can reduce future expenses and improve heating and cooling efficiency over time.

The article concludes that evaluating HVAC system age, maintenance history, repair frequency, and overall home comfort helps homeowners make informed decisions. By carefully weighing repair vs replace HVAC options, homeowners can better manage costs and system reliability. Consulting a qualified HVAC Expert is recommended to assess current performance and provide a clear path forward based on individual needs.

Should You Repair or Replace Your HVAC System? What Homeowners Should Consider First features insights from Leslie Roe, an HVAC expert at Precision Plumbing and Heating in Traverse City, Michigan, on HelloNation.

data.title: Ayrton Senna's style leads the Senna brand into fashion and lifestyle
data.description:
Ayrton Senna's style leads the Senna brand into fashion and lifestyle

Ayrton Senna's style leads the Senna brand into fashion and lifestyle

PR Newswire

SAO PAULO, Oct. 16, 2026

New collaborations connect fashion and motorsport to reach new audiences: five in 10 Americans who know the three-time Formula One world champion also see him as a fashion inspiration

SAO PAULO, Oct. 16, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Senna, the brand that represents the values of three-time Formula One world champion Ayrton Senna, is expanding into fashion and lifestyle. This month it launched its first global collection with Zara, one of the world's largest fashion retailers. The collection is available at Zara.com and in 200 selected stores worldwide. The brand will also release custom sneakers with Chummy's Customs and new official collections at SennaShop.com, including a collaboration with Classic Team Lotus.

The move follows a shift in how people relate to Senna today. Five in 10 Americans who know Senna see him as a fashion inspiration, according to a survey conducted by Senna Brands in the United States. Many of them never saw him race.

"A lot of people meet Ayrton today through a TV series, a photograph, a jacket, and not on a racetrack," said Bianca Senna, global CEO of Senna Brands. "Fashion lets us meet them where they already are, with products that carry what he stood for: overcoming limits, excellence and constant evolution."

Ayrton Senna won 41 races and three world championships in Formula One, the top tier of international motor racing. Off the track, his style was simple and consistent: jeans, polo shirts, a leather jacket. The Zara collection draws on one of his best-known images, in which he wears jeans and '90s sunglasses, has a jacket over his shoulder and carries a briefcase, with a plane behind him.

The 17-piece collection includes a minimalist black leather jacket inspired by one he wore, a Prince of Wales check blazer, the polo shirts associated with his public image and racing jackets carrying the Senna logo.

Later this year, the brand will release a collaboration with Chummy's Customs, a studio that hand-customizes sneakers. The limited editions, of 500 pairs, carry references to Senna's career. At SennaShop.com, a new collection made in official partnership with Classic Team Lotus, the team Senna drove for in Formula One from 1985 to 1987, features design elements from its iconic cars.

Senna is present in more than 70 countries, and the new launches join a partner portfolio that includes TAG Heuer, McLaren, Ducati and recent launches with LEGO and Sea-Doo. In Brazil, the brand also works with Asics and New Era Cap. More collaborations will be announced in 2027, taking Ayrton Senna's name from the starting grid to the streets.

"Fashion is looking back at the '90s, and Formula One has a new generation of fans. Ayrton sits right where those two meet," said Bianca Senna. "He never dressed to make a statement, and that is exactly why his style still works."

About Senna brand
Senna is a global brand that connects the legacy and values of three-time Formula 1 World Champion Ayrton Senna to audiences around the world, inspiring generations to become the best version of themselves. Founded in 1990, the brand today spans more than 60 partners with a direct presence in over 70 countries through licensed products and strategic collaborations. Brand royalties help fund Instituto Ayrton Senna, supporting public education in Brazil for over 30 years.

data.title: AM Best Revises Outlooks to Positive, Affirms Credit Ratings of BTG Pactual Resseguradora S.A. and BTG Pactual Seguros S.A.
data.description:
AM Best Revises Outlooks to Positive, Affirms Credit Ratings of BTG Pactual Resseguradora S.A. and BTG Pactual Seguros S.A.

AM Best has revised the outlooks to positive from stable and affirmed the Financial Strength Rating of B++ (Good) and the Long-Term Issuer Credit Rating of “bbb+” (Good) of BTG Pactual Resseguradora S.A. (BTG Re) (São Paulo, Brazil) and BTG Pactual Seguros S.A. (BTG Seguros) (São Paulo, Brazil). Concurrently, AM Best has affirmed the Brazil National Scale Rating (NSR) of “aaa.BR” (Exceptional) of BTG Re and BTG Seguros. The outlook of this NSR is stable.

The Credit Ratings (ratings) reflect BTG Re’s balance sheet strength, which AM Best assesses as very strong, as well as its adequate operating performance, neutral business profile and appropriate enterprise risk management.

The positive outlooks on these ratings reflect AM Best’s expectation that BTG Re will maintain its risk-adjusted capitalization at the strongest level, as measured by Best’s Capital Adequacy Ratio (BCAR), supported by the initiatives implemented by its management.

BTG Re is a domestic reinsurer in Brazil, operating predominantly in the surety segments in Brazil, Latin America, and recently, in Portugal and Spain, as part of its expansion strategy. The company also recently entered the agricultural line through business assumed from its affiliated company, TOO Seguros S.A. BTG Re’s intermediate parent, Banco BTG Pactual S.A. (BTG Pactual) [B3: BPAC11], provides operational support and risk management capabilities and can provide liquidity if needed.

Also reflected in BTG Re’s ratings is the impact of its credit profile and Brazil’s challenging and volatile macroeconomic and political environment, which continues to hamper meaningful economic recovery and stability in the country. BTG Pactual has shown a consistent trend in its results and credit strength while expanding and diversifying its operations; however, BTG Re’s ratings are somewhat limited by its domestic operating environment.

BTG Re maintains solid standalone attributes in terms of operating performance, including low loss and expense ratios, and the strongest level of risk-adjusted capitalization, as measured by BCAR. BTG Re has produced positive earnings since inception, driven by underwriting results and investment income. BTG Re also benefits from a solid retrocession program that mitigates its underwriting exposures; the company’s reinsurance retention remains low.

BTG Seguros is a domestic insurer in Brazil, operating predominantly in the country’s surety segment. The company takes advantage of the business profile and market presence of its affiliated company, BTG Re, to which it cedes almost all of its risk.

BTG Seguros maintains adequate standalone attributes in terms of operating performance, including low loss and expense ratios, and the strongest level of risk-adjusted capitalization, as measured by BCAR. BTG Seguros has produced positive earnings in recent years, mainly driven by investment income. AM Best’s analysis of BTG Seguros and BTG Re benefits from BTG Pactual’s expertise, stemming from its long track record with a portfolio of large companies.

AM Best continues to monitor BTG Seguros and BTG Re’s balance sheet strength, operating performance, risk-adjusted capitalization and the execution of its product and geographic expansion, along with the credit profile of its parent.

Positive rating actions could take place if the company sustains its balance sheet strength at the strongest level or better in the intermediate term. Negative rating actions could take place if a deterioration in its business profile occurs due to volatility in the country’s economy, which could affect the company’s performance.

This press release relates to Credit Ratings that have been published on AM Best’s website. For all rating information relating to the release and pertinent disclosures, including details of the office responsible for issuing each of the individual ratings referenced in this release, please see AM Best’s Recent Rating Activity web page. For additional information regarding the use and limitations of Credit Rating opinions, please view Guide to Best’s Credit Ratings. For information on the proper use of Best’s Credit Ratings, Best’s Performance Assessments, Best’s Preliminary Credit Assessments and AM Best press releases, please view Guide to Proper Use of Best’s Ratings & Assessments.

AM Best is a global credit rating agency, news publisher and data analytics provider specializing in the insurance industry. Headquartered in the United States, the company does business in over 100 countries with regional offices in London, Amsterdam, Dubai, Hong Kong, Singapore and Mexico City.
